subject: English
passage:
Text 1
The naturalist Kavita Han once claimed that field biology is the most accessible of scientific disciplines to practice. While researchers in other sciences—particle physics, molecular genetics, oceanography—require expensive equipment and institutional laboratories to conduct their work, amateur naturalists can observe, as Han said, "during a lunch break, from a backyard window, along a commute, and in notebooks kept beside the kettle." So amateurs can produce worthwhile scientific observations even if they must earn their living in another occupation.

Text 2
Any assessment of contemporary ecological research must reckon with the professionalization of the field. While it is possible in theory for anyone to publish in Ecology Letters, Journal of Animal Ecology, or a similar major outlet, most people who do so have advanced degrees and sustained access to institutional datasets, which requires time not often available to those who must also work full-time jobs. Thus, financial security indirectly affects who becomes a contributor to ecological knowledge.
prompt: Based on the texts, how would Han (Text 1) most likely respond to the argument presented in Text 2?

choices.A: By indicating that amateur naturalists who publish in major ecology journals are most likely to be able to earn a living through their scientific work.
choices.B: By pointing out that people can produce valuable scientific observations in circumstances other than those described by the author of Text 2.
choices.C: By suggesting that scientists who specialize in more resource-intensive disciplines are unlikely to also be successful as field naturalists.
choices.D: By asserting that people often take full-time jobs in order to afford the advanced degrees described in Text 2.

explanation:
Choice B is the best answer because it reflects how Han would most likely respond to the argument presented in Text 2. In Text 1, Han argues that field biology is the most accessible of scientific disciplines because amateur naturalists can observe in fragmented moments—"during a lunch break, from a backyard window, along a commute, and in notebooks kept beside the kettle"—and can therefore produce "worthwhile scientific observations even if they must earn their living in another occupation." Text 2, by contrast, argues that contemporary ecological research has become professionalized and that publishing in major outlets typically requires advanced degrees and institutional access unavailable to those working full-time jobs, concluding that "financial security indirectly affects who becomes a contributor to ecological knowledge." Han would most likely respond by pointing out that valuable scientific observations can be produced in circumstances other than those described by the author of Text 2—namely, in the brief moments available to amateurs who must work full-time jobs.

Why C is incorrect:

Choice C is incorrect because neither text discusses whether scientists in other disciplines would be unlikely to succeed as field naturalists. Text 1 briefly mentions particle physics, molecular genetics, and oceanography only to contrast their equipment and institutional requirements with field biology's accessibility, not to suggest that practitioners of those fields would fail as amateur naturalists.
